title: Delayed Cancer Treatment. Missed Medication. How a Popular Insurance Plan’s Use of Prior Authorization Hurt Patients.
author: Brandon Roberts
content:
Felicia tried everything she could think of to get her insurer to cover the
only treatment that made a difference in her years-long effort to manage her
obesity.

In 2024, after her insurer denied her coverage for medication despite her
doctor’s order, the 38-year-old Texan sought the help of consumer advocates.
She crafted a detailed appeal. She sent it not just to the head of the Fortune
500 company that oversaw her health insurance plan, but also copied the
secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the chair of
the Federal Trade Commission.

A short time later, someone called from a number she didn’t recognize. It was
Kevin Counihan, CEO of her health plan, Ambetter.

Felicia, who asked to be identified by her middle name due to her fear of
reprisals and so that she could share sensitive medical information, calmly
told Counihan that she hoped that “something gets done right by me and by my
health.”

“I have tried everything in the formulary. I exhausted all options,” she
explained on the call, which she recorded and shared with ProPublica.

![A man with gray hair wearing a black suit and red tie crosses his arms and
looks directly at the camera. He stands in a building with glass
walls.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/GettyImages-541017452-vert-
crop_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=527)Kevin
Counihan, who was CEO of Ambetter and had once overseen the federal Affordable
Care Act marketplace, conceded that a customer’s reported experience with his
company had been “a tremendous inconvenience and a real pain in the neck.”
Brooks Kraft/Getty Images

A veteran health insurance executive who had once overseen the federal
Affordable Care Act marketplace, Counihan conceded on the call that Felicia’s
reported experience with his company had been “a tremendous inconvenience and
a real pain in the neck.” But he assured her that “we really want to get you
what you” and your doctor “think is the most appropriate medication for you.”

“I’m working on it as fast as possible,” said Counihan.

Counihan’s call was a rare acknowledgment from the company’s top brass of a
pervasive problem. Ambetter, the most popular plan on the ACA marketplace, has
one of the worst track records of delaying or denying medical coverage by
refusing to cover the costs.

ProPublica has found that Ambetter last year denied these kinds of requests —
known as prior authorization — at a higher rate than any other large insurer
on the ACA marketplace. Our analysis of Ambetter’s own data, along with
interviews with more than two dozen recent customers, sheds new light on the
vast and sometimes illogical nature of how the company can block access to
care.

Each dot below is a marketplace plan in Texas, sized according to the number
of prior authorization requests it reported in 2025. Plans further to the
right deny those requests at higher rates. Ambetter plans are shown in red.

![A bubble chart of the denial rates of prior authorization requests made to
marketplace plans in Texas. Most of the bubbles are gray, but two to the far
right are red. The rates range from about 1% to 32%. Four small plans deny
less than 5% of prior authorization requests, one mid-size plan denies about
13% and three deny between 22% and 24%. The two plans farthest to the right
are Ambetter plans, which are colored red and placed at about 32%. The plan
furthest to the right is labeled “Ambetter from Superior HealthPlan, 218K
requests.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/fallback-1-prior-auth-
ambetter_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_quality_95_embedColorProfile_true.jpg?w=752)

In Texas, where Ambetter’s denial rates were above 32%, the company initially
refused to pay for a medical scan for a patient with Stage 4 colon cancer
because the doctor hadn’t ordered a cheaper, less precise scan first.

![The chart switches to Iowa’s three marketplace plans. A large gray plan
denies about 11% of requests and a very small one about 12%. The labeled red
circle, Ambetter Health \(Iowa Total Care\) with 3.2K requests, sits far to
the right at 31%, nearly triple the other plans’
rates.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/fallback-2-prior-auth-
ambetter_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_quality_95_embedColorProfile_true.jpg?w=752)

In Iowa, where Ambetter’s denial rate was 31%, it approved a patient’s
colonoscopy but denied a request for the bowel prep that all patients must
drink in advance of the procedure.

![The chart switches to Kansas’ four marketplace plans. Three gray plans deny
between about 4% and 14% of requests. The labeled red circle, Ambetter from
Sunflower Health with 64K requests, is the largest plan in the state and sits
well to the right at 26%.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/fallback-3-prior-auth-
ambetter_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_quality_95_embedColorProfile_true.jpg?w=752)

In Kansas, where Ambetter’s denial rate was 26%, it stopped covering an anti-
inflammatory treatment for a patient with Crohn’s disease because it wanted
the patient to try a different drug.

![The chart zooms out to all 19 states where Ambetter reported data, listed
from Texas at the top down to Florida, ordered by Ambetter’s denial rate. A
size key shows circles for 50K, 100K and 200K requests. In most states, the
red Ambetter circle is the farthest right in its row. Gray plans are scattered
mostly between 5% and 20%. Together, the red circles form a band running from
about 33% in Texas down to about 21% in Florida. Running vertically down the
chart are two dashed lines: a black line at 16% labeled “All plans avg.” and a
red line at 25% labeled “Ambetter avg.” Nearly all red Ambetter circles fall
to the right of the 16% line and cluster around the 25% line, while most gray
circles fall to the left of 16%. At the bottom is a note that reads “Source:
ProPublica analysis of 2025 prior authorization disclosures from AuthDenied
and insurance companies, including 21 Ambetter plans and 93 other plans.
Denial rate is the standard denial rate as published by insurers. Urgent prior
authorization denials reported separately are not
included.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/fallback-4-prior-auth-
ambetter_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_quality_95_embedColorProfile_true.jpg?w=752)

A ProPublica analysis of nearly 200 federal marketplace plans across the
country found that Ambetter had the highest denial rates in most states where
it provided data.

Ambetter plans had an average denial rate of 25% in states where the company
reported data for last year. That’s substantially higher than the 16% average
denial rate for all marketplace plans.

Our analysis is [based on data](https://www.authdenied.com/) that federal
regulators required marketplace plans to report and publish for the first time
this year. The requirement is intended to offer greater transparency into how
often insurers restrict care by denying prior authorization for treatment.

Since the ACA marketplace launched in 2013, there has been little transparency
around how often insurers request — and deny — prior authorization. Insurers
use prior authorization to limit spending on treatment, equipment and
prescriptions. They say it is also intended to ensure that doctors try less
expensive and less invasive treatments before pricier ones. Health insurance
experts said that the process of how or when prior authorization gets used is
largely a black box.

U.S. Rep. Craig Goldman, a Republican from Texas, sponsored a bipartisan bill
that would require marketplace plans to disclose more information about their
use of prior authorization. “These companies represent these individuals — and
yet denying them coverage and not being transparent with what they will be
able to cover,” he said. “They’re just not there for the best interest of the
people.”

Four former heads of state insurance departments who reviewed ProPublica’s
findings said that Ambetter’s high denial rate was such an outlier that
current regulators should examine further.

“This is stunning — and not in a good way,” Mila Kofman, a former insurance
superintendent in Maine who now oversees the District of Columbia’s ACA
marketplace, said of Ambetter’s denial rate. “This is something insurance
regulators need to understand. There’s a huge opportunity for regulators to
address the improper use of prior authorization.”

## [We’re Investigating Prior Authorization. Help ProPublica Understand Your
Health Insurance Denial.](https://www.propublica.org/getinvolved/propublica-
health-insurance-prior-authorization-reporting)

ProPublica is looking into the ways health insurers’ use of prior
authorization impacts patients. We need your help to figure out if the process
is still leading to delayed or missed treatments, tests, medical equipment or
medication.

[Share Your Experience](https://www.propublica.org/getinvolved/propublica-
health-insurance-prior-authorization-reporting)

Sarah London, CEO of Ambetter’s parent company, Centene, recently said in a
statement on its website that it was “[creating a more predictable and
transparent experience](https://www.centene.com/news/ahip-partnerships-prior-
authorization_progress.html)” for its customers. That statement followed
growing backlash against the industry and a push to limit the practice of
prior authorization.

Last year Centene joined America’s largest insurers in vowing to rely on prior
authorization less often. Industry representatives have said that the
collective efforts of those insurers [will decrease their use of prior
authorization across all of their plans by
11%](https://content.naic.org/sites/default/files/call_materials/priorauth-
industry-reform-initiative-naic-rftf-6-29-26.pdf) in 2026. (Health plans
aren’t required to publish 2026 data until next year.)

ProPublica sent Centene a detailed list of questions about its use of prior
authorization and the impact it has on its customers. ProPublica also provided
Ambetter with signed releases from customers, including Felicia, waiving their
right to privacy, so that Centene representatives could speak with ProPublica
about their specific denials. Centene didn’t respond to ProPublica’s
questions. In a statement, a spokesperson for the company said that Ambetter
is “committed to help ensure patients receive safe, appropriate, evidence-
based care, and we continue to work to simplify the prior authorization
process and reduce administrative burden for members and providers.”

Reached by phone, Counihan told ProPublica that he retired this year and
declined to comment due to “contractual commitments” with the company that
prevent him from doing so.

### Listen to Ambetter’s Then-CEO

Kevin Counihan tells a customer he can’t approve coverage of the treatment her
doctor sought.

**Kevin Counihan:** I have taken this whole issue, uh, all the way through our
medical directors and, uh, policy people and everywhere, and I’m — I’m sorry
and disappointed to tell you that I don’t have approval to have this covered.
Obtained by ProPublica

For some Ambetter customers, the consequences of prior authorization denials
were particularly stark, leading to delayed tests and disrupted treatments. A
small fraction of those customers got Ambetter to cover their care after
complaining to powerful politicians. One Ambetter customer who was denied
routine bloodwork complained to a state agency. Another who had been denied
cancer treatment asked a U.S. senator for help.

Even though Felicia’s complaint made it all the way up to powerful politicians
— and she had pressed Centene’s C-suite to get in touch — she was disheartened
by what Counihan ultimately would have to say.

Felicia had lost track of all the hours spent on curbing her weight, going so
far as to try three different anti-obesity medications. During the follow-up
call, Counihan explained that didn’t actually have the authority to help with
the fourth.

“Do what you need to do,” Counihan responded. “Escalate it in any way that you
can.”

* * *

![A girl with short brown hair wears a long red shirt and jeans as she sits at
a full drum kit in a yellow room. A man wearing a bandana on his head sits
next to her and smiles. Drum pads, various instruments and posters decorate
the room.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/11102026-Odom-Prior-
Auth-004_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Jones
at home with his 13-year-old daughter, Makenna Jones, as she plays the drums.
He spent much of this year undergoing cancer treatment. Matt Odom for
ProPublica

This spring, as Richie Jones recovered from having his tumor-filled prostate
removed, he received some troubling news. The cancer was still in his body.

The 49-year-old drummer from Atlanta’s suburbs was willing to do anything to
get more time with his wife and daughter. His oncologist said the best option
was to shoot a pencil-sized beam of protons at the cancer that remained,
zapping it out of existence. That kind of therapy can cost far more than
standard radiation but inflicts far less damage to the rest of the body.

First, though, his oncologist had to confirm that Ambetter would cover proton
therapy. He asked the insurer to approve it in advance, as it required.
Ambetter denied the request based on a recommendation from an oncologist
working with the insurer.

Insurers have varying policies on whether to cover proton therapy for patients
with prostate cancer. In recent years, insurance researchers have found that
patients with commercial plans who are facing a denial for proton therapy for
a variety of cancers have a good shot of getting it overturned on appeal.

Jones’ oncologist appealed. That, too, was denied. Ambetter explained its
decision in a letter to Jones, claiming he did “not have a type of cancer this
treatment is used for.”

What angered Jones most was that there was a different doctor advising
Ambetter on the denial of the appeal, and that doctor didn’t specialize in
proton therapy, let alone cancer. It was an OB-GYN.

Fearful that his cancer would spread more, Jones emailed Ambetter’s support
department, hoping to break through to whatever human was on the other end.
“You have the power to allow my child to have her daddy around for years to
come,” he wrote.

When people actually fight prior authorization denials, they have a good shot
at winning. ProPublica’s analysis found that more than half of Ambetter
customers who contested their denials had them overturned. But the vast
majority of the time, denials go uncontested. Only 7% of prior authorization
denials by Ambetter were challenged last year, the analysis found.

Marketplace plan holders told ProPublica that they didn’t appeal because they
didn’t know about their rights or how to navigate the process. Insurance
experts and advocates say that patience and persistence are required to fight
a denial.

### Ambetter Customers Have a Good Shot at Overturning Their Denials. Few of
Them Try.

Most prior authorization denials are never appealed. More often than not,
Ambetter customers who appeal get approved after going through a complex
process.

![A visualization of two crowds where each person represents 100 insurance
denials. On the left, under the heading Ambetter Plans, roughly 190 figures
are represented. On the right, under the heading Other Plans, roughly 31
people are shown. In both groups, more than 90% of the figures are gray,
representing denials that were not appealed. The remaining figures are green
or red, indicating appeals either won or lost.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/fallback-crowd-prior-auth-
ambetter_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_quality_95_embedColorProfile_true.jpg?w=752)Source:
ProPublica analysis of 2025 prior authorization disclosures from
[AuthDenied](https://www.authdenied.com/) and insurance companies, including
21 Ambetter plans and 93 other plans. Figures from Wee People by ProPublica
and Alberto Cairo. Brandon Roberts/ProPublica

On the other side of metro Atlanta from Jones, 48-year-old artist Travis
Christopher was trying to get treatment for his liver cancer last year. After
getting so sick that he left his job — and lost the insurance that came with
it — he bought an Ambetter plan on the marketplace.

It covered a specialized treatment by his oncologist, who placed a wire of
irradiated beads in his liver to precisely target his tumor. But to know if
the radiation worked, his oncologist needed CT scans.

Ambetter denied three different requests for prior authorization for the
scans. After a month of delays, Christopher complained to his state senator,
saying that he was “stuck waiting until Ambetter decides whether or not I live
or die.” The state senator passed it along to Georgia’s insurance
commissioner. Soon after, Ambetter overturned the denial and agreed to cover
the care.

Every day of delay can increase the odds that cancer spreads. No one can say
how much the wait affected Christopher’s prognosis. What is certain is that
Christopher’s health got worse in the months ahead. He died this past winter,
shortly after his daughter was born.

![A man with a beard and brown hair wears glasses and a suit with a purple
tie. He smiles at the camera.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/travis-christopher-
obit_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg)Travis
Christopher complained to his state senator that Ambetter had denied three
requests for cancer scans. Courtesy of the Christopher family

Jones was able to get care in time. Like Christopher, he worked to draw
attention to Ambetter’s denial. He contacted local journalists, wrote to the
office of the U.S. Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, and filed a complaint with
Georgia’s insurance commissioner. In late June, after getting in touch with
staffers in both officials’ offices, Jones received a call from Emory
Healthcare: Their oncologists were ready to start.

Ambetter had decided to reverse its denial.

Over the course of his nearly 40 rounds of proton therapy, Jones realized that
he wanted others to know the importance of fighting back. So he granted
permission to Ossoff to publish what had happened in a [report on prior
authorization denials](https://www.ossoff.senate.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/26.08.31_Sen.-Ossoff-Report%E2%80%94Insurance-
Companies-Denying-Necessary-Health-Care.pdf). In a statement to ProPublica,
Ossoff said that he has “heard from too many Georgians who get a cancer
diagnosis, and then instead of being free to fight their cancer, they have to
fight their insurance company.”

“We need to ban health insurance companies from denying or delaying needed
health care,” Ossoff said in the statement.

Several months later, Jones stood in the lobby of Emory’s cancer center.
Surrounded by his family and friends, he rang a ceremonial bell hanging on the
wall, marking the end of his treatment.

It was only after he was in remission that Jones would begin to see just how
much his complaint had mattered.

With Jones’ permission, ProPublica obtained records this month that shed light
on why Ambetter changed its decision about the proton therapy. The records
include a letter Ambetter sent to Georgia’s insurance commissioner’s office
that explained the rationale for each of its denials. In the letter, the
insurer wrote that it had decided, two days after Jones filed his complaint,
to consult clinical guidelines used by America’s leading oncologists in
determining how to proceed with covering his treatment. Ambetter previously
had relied on a more restrictive guideline from a contractor that handles its
prior authorization requests for cancer treatment.

“Why wasn’t that their guideline in the first place?” Jones said. “Why does it
take being a squeaky wheel to have them change their mind?”

![A man wearing a bandana over his head sits in a desk chair with his chin in
his left hand, while holding a pair of glasses in the same hand. The room is
full of yellow legal pads, paper and art supplies, and a drafting table has
drawings of owls on it.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/11102026-Odom-Prior-
Auth-040_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=2560)Jones
at his drafting table in his art studio at home this month. He is a visual
artist as well as a performer and percussion teacher. Matt Odom for ProPublica

* * *

In June 2025, following a meeting with U.S. Health and Human Services
Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Centene and other large insurers promised [to
reduce the volume of medical services subject to prior
authorization](http://ahip.org/news/press-releases/health-plans-take-action-
to-simplify-prior-authorization). Centene has since touted “[measurable
progress](https://www.centene.com/news/ahip-partnerships-prior-
authorization_progress.html)” toward fulfilling that promise. The company
didn’t answer ProPublica’s questions about whether Ambetter’s prior
authorization use has gone down this year.

But insurance experts, consumer advocates and lawmakers question how far those
promises go.

Wendell Potter, a former Cigna executive turned consumer advocate, recently
wrote that these commitments rely on “[an impressive-sounding number to
mislead.](https://healthcareuncovered.substack.com/p/pr-stunt-unitedhealths-
big-prior)” For instance, he said that UnitedHealthcare promised a 30% drop in
prior authorization requirements, but only 2% of covered medical services are
eligible for the more relaxed requirements. (UnitedHealthcare spokesperson
Eric Hausman told ProPublica that the insurer has been “transparent” about its
efforts to reduce the use of prior authorization and has already enacted some
of them.)

Brit Vanneman, a staff attorney for the National Health Law Program, wrote
that these commitments “[may simply be a strategic attempt to deflect growing
public criticism](https://healthlaw.org/voluntary-industry-prior-
authorization-commitments-empty-promises-little-accountability/)” regarding
prior authorization.

“The commitments are vague,” Vanneman told ProPublica. “There’s a lot of
fluff.”

What isn’t vague: the continued impact of prior authorization denials since
the industry’s pledge.

> “I still do not have a CT scan scheduled, and am stuck waiting until
> Ambetter decides whether or not I live or die.”
>
> Travis Christopher, in an email to his state senator in September 2025

Two women got their denials overturned by Ambetter only after posting about
them on social media. One, a Florida mother, told ProPublica she bought an
Ambetter plan because her previous insurer stopped covering autism therapy for
her 6-year-old son. The Ambetter plan she chose had covered other children
seen by the providers who’d treated her son for the past two years. But
Ambetter denied the request for his treatment this year, and her son’s care
was put on pause.

The other, a Kansas woman, said Ambetter denied a drug infusion to treat her
Crohn’s disease last year. She said this was shocking to her, since for the
previous two years Ambetter had covered the infusion, which worked better for
her than anything else she tried.

Both women’s social media posts prompted Ambetter reps to reach out to them
directly, saying they wanted to address their problems. And indeed, the
ordered treatments were provided.

Felicia wasn’t as fortunate. After Ambetter’s CEO expressed sympathy and
encouraged her to fight for her obesity treatment, she moved forward with the
final step in the process: asking an independent company to review her appeal.

At that point, Felicia had spent two years on three different weight-loss
drugs that were covered by Ambetter, including the popular GLP-1 drug Ozempic.
But those drugs had caused side effects, such as insomnia and migraines. When
she was prescribed samples of tirzepatide, another GLP-1, by her doctor in
2023, everything finally clicked: She lost a significant amount of weight over
two months without any side effects.

But Ambetter was not willing to cover Zepbound, the tirzepatide her doctor
prescribed.

As a way to keep costs down, health insurers tend to deny requests for GLP-1s
not listed on their formularies. When that happens, a customer can appeal and
seek a formulary exception.

In September 2024, she asked her endocrinologist to support her appeal. He
explained in a letter that a denial of this particular GLP-1 “could
significantly hinder her progress and potentially lead to worsening of her
condition, which could result in more intensive and costly interventions in
the future.” As he saw it, this GLP-1 was “the most appropriate and
potentially life-saving medication,” especially given Felicia’s other
overlapping medical conditions.

But that November, the company overseeing the independent review declined to
consider her appeal, writing that an appeal involving a medication that wasn’t
on a health plan’s approved drug list was “outside of our scope of review.” In
other words, Felicia had hit a dead end.

Felicia has continued struggling with obesity ever since the Zepbound denial.
She’s also experienced worsening symptoms for several other chronic
conditions, including persistent migraines. Felicia said she has nine each
month on average, and medical experts say that obesity is a strong risk factor
for migraines. But Ambetter has denied prior authorization for numerous
migraine medications prescribed by her doctors.

Ambetter is the only insurance Felicia had ever bought. By this fall, she had
become so fed up with the denials that she contacted an insurance broker to
help her find another marketplace plan during open enrollment. But the quotes
she received for various plans were either much higher than Ambetter’s or
didn’t provide access to her doctors. If she wanted to clear the hurdles she’d
faced, the cost would be far more than she could possibly afford.

It left her with a sinking feeling: Ambetter might be her only viable option.

The post [Delayed Cancer Treatment. Missed Medication. How a Popular Insurance
Plan’s Use of Prior Authorization Hurt
Patients.](https://www.propublica.org/article/ambetter-prior-authorization-
denials) appeared first on [ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
